# <mark>AIDS-Associated Kaposi Sarcoma</mark>

## <mark>EPIDEMIOLOGY</mark>

A major harbinger of the AIDS pandemic was the emergence of clusters of young homosexual men suffering from Kaposi sarcoma (KS) in large U.S. cities in 1981. During the first decade of the AIDS pandemic, KS was diagnosed as the AIDS-defining illness in more than 20 percent of HIV-1-infected patients in Europe. Despite a decline in recent years, KS remains the most frequent AIDS-associated tumor in men who have sex with men. Other patient groups at risk for AIDS—including intravenous drug users, hemophiliacs, blood transfusion recipients, and children born to HIV-positive mothers in industrialized countries—are far less commonly affected.

The situation differs in Africa, where KS is the most common tumor among HIV-1-infected individuals across all risk groups, including children with AIDS.

## <mark>CLINICAL FEATURES</mark>

<mark>AIDS-associated KS differs from classic KS by its more rapid progression and multifocal dissemination.</mark> <mark>Early lesions appear as small, oval, violaceous macules that quickly evolve into plaques and nodules.</mark> <mark>These lesions are often present at multiple sites at disease onset and tend to progress rapidly.</mark>

<mark>In contrast to other forms of KS, initial lesions in AIDS patients frequently develop on the face—particularly the nose, eyelids, and ears—and on the trunk, where they often align along the skin’s relaxed tension lines (Fig.</mark> 128-3). <mark>If left untreated, disseminated lesions may coalesce into large plaques affecting extensive areas of the face, trunk, or extremities, potentially causing functional impairments.</mark>

<mark>Oral mucosal involvement is common and is the presenting site in 10% to 15% of AIDS-related KS cases (Fig.</mark> 128-4). <mark>Pharyngeal involvement may also occur, leading to difficulties in eating, speaking, and breathing.</mark>

## EXTRACUTANEOUS INVOLVEMENT

Extra-cutaneous involvement occurs more rapidly and severely in AIDS-associated KS compared to classic KS. In addition to the oral mucosa, KS lesions are most frequently found in lymph nodes, the gastrointestinal tract, and the lungs.

Although gastrointestinal KS typically occurs alongside cutaneous disease, isolated gastrointestinal involvement can occur. The stomach and duodenum are common sites, and lesions in these areas may cause symptoms such as gastrointestinal bleeding or obstruction. These submucosal lesions are often visible during gastroscopy but may be missed on biopsy due to their depth.

Pulmonary KS can lead to respiratory symptoms including bronchospasm, cough, and progressive respiratory insufficiency. Diagnosis is best achieved via bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy.

## DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

Differential diagnoses for cutaneous KS vary depending on the clinical stage and are outlined in Box 128-1.

## <mark>HISTOPATHOLOGY</mark>

<mark>The histopathologic features of KS depend on the stage of lesion development.</mark> <mark>Early patch-stage lesions show subtle changes, primarily an increase in dermal vasculature lined by slightly atypical endothelial cells (Fig.</mark> 128-5).

# <mark>Classic Kaposi Sarcoma</mark>

## <mark>EPIDEMIOLOGY</mark>  
The annual incidence rates for classic Kaposi sarcoma (KS) vary significantly across geographic regions, ranging from 0.14 per million inhabitants in Great Britain to 10.5 per million in men and 2.7 per million in women in Italy. A marked male predominance has been consistently observed since the initial descriptions of the disease, with a male-to-female ratio of approximately 3:1 in most large studies. The higher incidence in countries bordering the Mediterranean Sea has led some researchers to propose a "Mediterranean variant" of KS as a distinct entity. However, due to similarities in clinical course and behavior, this variant is not considered separately from classic KS.

## <mark>CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS</mark>  
The typical patient with classic KS is a Caucasian male in his sixth decade of life, often with Mediterranean or Jewish ancestry. Lesions usually begin on the skin of the distal lower extremities—particularly the dorsum of the feet—as unilateral or bilateral bluish-red macules that may resemble hematomas. These lesions progress slowly, both horizontally and vertically, evolving into firm plaques and eventually into nodules. Over time, the color of the lesions changes to brown, and the overlying skin becomes hyperkeratotic. Ulceration is common, especially on the lower limbs. Perilesional pitting edema is frequently present and may progress to fibrosis.

Classic KS generally follows an indolent course, with gradual proximal extension over years or even decades. Many patients live with slowly progressive disease for extended periods. After several years, visceral dissemination may occur, with involvement of lymph nodes, mucous membranes, and internal organs—particularly the gastrointestinal tract—though gastrointestinal lesions are often asymptomatic. Given the advanced age of most affected individuals, death from unrelated causes frequently precedes widespread disease progression.

# African Endemic Kaposi Sarcoma

## EPIDEMIOLOGY  
An increased incidence of Kaposi sarcoma among Black Africans in Central Africa was recognized decades before the emergence of the AIDS pandemic. In some countries in this region, KS accounts for up to 10% of all malignancies in men. There is a strong male predominance, with male-to-female ratios ranging from 3:1 in children to as high as 18:1 in adults. The age at onset is lower than in classic KS, with significant presentation in younger adults and even children.

# <mark>HISTOPATHOLOGY</mark>

<mark>The histopathology of Kaposi sarcoma (KS) varies according to the stage of disease development.</mark>  

<mark>**Patch Stage:**</mark>  
Early patch-like lesions show subtle histopathologic changes, primarily characterized by an increase in the number of dermal vessels lined by slightly atypical endothelial cells (Fig. 128-5). <mark>These vessels are predominantly located in the superficial dermis, run parallel to the skin surface, and often form irregular, slit-like or cleft-like spaces.</mark> Focal hemosiderin deposits, extravasated red blood cells, and a moderate inflammatory infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and plasma cells are commonly seen in the surrounding tissue. <mark>Key differential diagnoses at this stage include **lymphangioma** and **granulation tissue**.</mark>

<mark>**Plaque Stage:**</mark>  
<mark>KS plaques exhibit more distinctive features, with extensive vascular proliferation throughout all levels of the dermis.</mark> <mark>There are numerous dilated and angulated vascular spaces that dissect collagen bundles, creating a spongy network of residual collagen.</mark> <mark>A hallmark of papular and plaque lesions is the presence of solid cords and fascicles of spindle cells intermixed with jagged vascular channels.</mark> <mark>This biphasic pattern—comprising both angiomatous and solid components—gradually evolves into a predominantly sarcomatous morphology as the disease progresses.</mark>

<mark>**Nodular Stage:**</mark>  
<mark>Nodular lesions are largely composed of proliferating spindle cells arranged in interlacing bundles and fascicles, with scattered, irregular, slit-like vascular spaces lacking well-defined endothelial linings.</mark> <mark>With advancing disease, these lesions may display marked nuclear pleomorphism, atypia, and increased mitotic activity.</mark> <mark>At the periphery of such tumors, areas resembling earlier KS stages—featuring abnormal vascular lumina, intravascular and extravasated erythrocytes, and siderophages—may persist.</mark> <mark>Erythrocytes are often entrapped within clefts formed by spindle cells and appear as eosinophilic globules; erythrophagocytosis can occasionally be observed.</mark> <mark>A mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, histiocytes, plasma cells, and occasionally neutrophils) is consistently present across all stages.</mark>

![Histopathology of Kaposi sarcoma – angiomatous and sarcomatous components](images/b0dfd4aca43615d16c86ab08e2cc7188b76be925c2daa4cde83a2ff67a928d95.jpg)  
<mark>*FIGURE 128-5: Biopsy from a nodular Kaposi sarcoma lesion showing both angiomatous areas resembling lymphangioma and solid, sarcomatous fascicles.*</mark>

---

# DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

Differential diagnoses for cutaneous and mucosal Kaposi sarcoma vary by clinical stage:

## Most Likely
- **Localized early disease:**  
  - Hematoma  
  - Stasis dermatitis  
  - Bacillary angiomatosis  
  - Pyogenic granuloma  
  - Well-differentiated angiosarcoma  

- **Advanced disease:**  
  - Acroangiodermatitis (pseudo-Kaposi)  
  - Bacillary angiomatosis  

- **Oropharyngeal lesions:**  
  - Non-Hodgkin lymphoma  
  - Squamous cell carcinoma  
  - Bacillary angiomatosis  

## Consider
- **Localized disease:**  
  - Dermatofibroma  
  - Melanoma  
  - Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans  
  - Leiomyosarcoma  
  - Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (in children)  
  - Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome  

- **Advanced disease:**  
  - Metastatic melanoma  
  - Cutaneous metastases from internal malignancies or leukemias  
  - Erythema elevatum et diutinum  
  - Angiosarcoma  

## Always Rule Out
- HIV-1 infection  
- Other causes of immunosuppression  
- Melanoma  

---

# TREATMENT

Treatment strategies for Kaposi sarcoma depend on the clinical type, extent of lesions, and organ systems involved.

Despite strong evidence implicating **human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8)** as the causative oncogenic agent in KS, antiherpetic therapies have not demonstrated consistent clinical efficacy and remain largely experimental.

## <mark>PCT-Like Syndromes and Differential Considerations</mark>

PCT-like syndromes have been reported in association with hepatic tumors and systemic lupus erythematosus. <mark>Subepidermal bullous dermatoses that clinically and histologically mimic porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) have also been described (see Pseudoporphyria).</mark> True PCT has been observed in patients with renal failure undergoing hemodialysis.

## <mark>Laboratory Findings in PCT</mark>

<mark>Confirmation of PCT relies on detecting markedly elevated plasma porphyrin levels—typically 5- to 100-fold higher than normal—and increased fecal excretion of isocoproporphyrin (ISOCOPRO).</mark>

### <mark>Urinary Porphyrin Excretion</mark>

<mark>Patients with PCT excrete increased amounts of porphyrins in the urine.</mark> <mark>In some cases, urine may exhibit a pink-red fluorescence under a Wood's lamp, although this finding is not always present.</mark>

<mark>The urinary porphyrin profile in PCT is characterized by three main features:</mark>
1. <mark>Elevated excretion of uroporphyrin (URO) and other acetate-substituted porphyrins.</mark>
2. <mark>A distinct isomer pattern of porphyrins, with mixtures of type I and type III isomers.</mark>
3. <mark>Increased fecal excretion of ISOCOPRO.</mark>

<mark>Urinary porphyrins in PCT include:</mark>
- <mark>Markedly increased 8-carboxyl URO</mark>
- <mark>Elevated 7-, 6-, and 5-carboxyl porphyrins</mark>
- <mark>Moderately increased 4-carboxyl porphyrin (COPRO), typically not exceeding 600 μg per 24 hours</mark>

<mark>The 8- and 7-carboxyl porphyrins constitute more than 90% of total urinary porphyrins.</mark> <mark>The isomer distribution is as follows:</mark>
- <mark>URO: ~60% type I, ~40% type III</mark>
- <mark>7- and 6-carboxyl porphyrins: >90% type III, <10% type I</mark>
- <mark>5- and 4-carboxyl porphyrins: ~50% each of type I and type III</mark>

<mark>This specific isomer pattern is consistently observed in PCT and aids in diagnosis.</mark>

### <mark>Fecal Porphyrin Excretion</mark>

<mark>In healthy individuals, uroporphyrin is present in stool only in trace amounts.</mark> <mark>In PCT, fecal porphyrin levels are elevated and primarily consist of:</mark>
- <mark>Isocoproporphyrin (ISOCOPRO), predominantly type III</mark>
- <mark>7-carboxyl porphyrin</mark>
- <mark>Smaller amounts of URO and COPRO</mark>

<mark>Total 24-hour fecal porphyrin excretion may exceed urinary excretion in PCT patients.</mark>

### Differentiation from Variegate Porphyria (VP)

<mark>The urinary URO-to-COPRO ratio is a useful diagnostic tool:</mark>
- <mark>In PCT: ratio is typically >3:1</mark>
- <mark>In VP: ratio is usually <1:1</mark>

<mark>In rare cases, patients with classic cutaneous features of PCT may have normal or only mildly elevated 24-hour urine porphyrin levels.</mark> In such instances, stool porphyrin analysis is essential, as fecal porphyrins are elevated in VP.

### <mark>Diagnostic Pitfalls and Confirmatory Testing</mark>

<mark>A negative urine fluorescent screening test does not rule out PCT.</mark> <mark>Some patients with clinical PCT may have normal screening results.</mark> <mark>Therefore, definitive diagnosis requires:</mark>
- <mark>Measurement of plasma porphyrin levels</mark>
- <mark>Quantitative 24-hour urine URO and COPRO analysis</mark>
- <mark>Stool PROTO and COPRO determinations</mark>

<mark>High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is preferred for accurate porphyrin speciation and differentiation between PCT and VP.</mark>

In rare cases of VP with normal fecal porphyrin excretion, bile porphyrin analysis may provide additional diagnostic clarity.

### <mark>Iron Overload in PCT</mark>

Virtually all patients with PCT exhibit iron overload, evidenced by:
- Elevated serum iron
- Increased ferritin levels
- Hepatocellular iron accumulation

Mild erythrocytosis may occasionally be present.

## Types of Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT)

### <mark>Acquired (Type I) PCT</mark>
<mark>In acquired (type I) PCT, uroporphyrinogen (UROGEN) decarboxylase deficiency is restricted to the liver.</mark> <mark>This tissue-specific deficiency may result from either a liver-specific gene defect or exposure to chemicals that selectively inhibit the hepatic form of the enzyme without affecting the erythrocyte (RBC) enzyme.</mark> <mark>Certain substances trigger PCT only in susceptible individuals—such as **alcohol** and **estrogens**—while others, like **hexachlorobenzene (HCB)**, can induce the disease in nearly all exposed individuals.</mark>

### Hereditary (Type II) PCT
Hereditary (type II) PCT is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by approximately 50% reduction in UROGEN decarboxylase activity across all tissues, including RBCs and cultured skin fibroblasts. Enzyme levels show a bimodal distribution:
- A large group (>80%) has normal enzyme concentration.
- A smaller group (<20%) exhibits about half the normal amount of detectable enzyme.

Some patients with type II PCT have enzyme activity at the lower end of the normal range. Clinical penetrance is low (~20%), indicating that most individuals with the genetic defect do not develop symptoms. This implies that additional genetic or environmental factors are required for disease expression. Over 100 mutations in the *UROGEN decarboxylase* gene have been identified, many of which impair enzyme stability or cause defective pre-mRNA splicing.

### Type III PCT
Not all patients with a family history of PCT have type II disease. Some individuals have multiple affected relatives but normal RBC UROGEN decarboxylase activity. This variant has been termed **type III PCT** by some researchers. Possible explanations include:
- Inheritance of a UROGEN decarboxylase variant that appears normal immunologically but is selectively vulnerable to hepatic inhibition.
- Presence of a second inherited enzyme defect unrelated to UROGEN decarboxylase.

These hypotheses remain under investigation.

### <mark>Differential Diagnosis and Dual Porphyrias</mark>
Some cases originally classified as hereditary PCT may actually represent **variegate porphyria (VP)**, another autosomal dominant porphyria. Families with both PCT and VP have been described ("dual porphyrias"). Additionally, coexistence of PCT and **acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)** has been reported, further complicating diagnosis and classification.

## <mark>Precipitating Factors in Acquired (Type I) PCT</mark>
Multiple agents and conditions are associated with the development of sporadic (type I) PCT:

- <mark>**Alcohol**</mark>
- **Estrogenic hormones**
- **Iron overload**
- **Viral infections** (hepatitis C, HIV)
- **Polychlorinated hydrocarbons** (e.g., HCB, TCDD)
- **Hemodialysis** in renal failure

### Alcohol
Alcohol consumption is a well-established trigger for PCT. Ethanol induces hepatic **ALA synthase**, the rate-limiting enzyme in heme synthesis. It also reduces erythrocyte UROGEN decarboxylase activity in both acute and chronic alcohol use. Ethanol inhibits other heme pathway enzymes, including **ferrochelatase** and **ALA dehydratase**. Chronic alcoholism suppresses erythropoiesis and increases intestinal iron absorption, effects potentially amplified by mutations linked to **hemochromatosis**.

### Table 132-6: Drugs and Chemicals Associated with PCT
- Ethyl alcohol  
- Estrogenic hormones  
- Hexachlorobenzene (HCB)  
- Chlorinated phenols  
- Iron  
- 2,3,7,8-Tetrachlorodibenzo-*p*-dioxin (TCDD)  
- Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs)  
- Herbicides: 2,4-dichloro- and 2,4,5-trichlorophenoxyacetic acid

## <mark>Reactive Skin and Joint Conditions in CSD</mark>

<mark>Reactive conditions involving the skin and joints can occur in patients with cat scratch disease (CSD).</mark>  
- <mark>**Erythema nodosum** develops in approximately **2%** of CSD patients.</mark>  
- **Rheumatoid factor-negative arthropathy** affects about **3%** of patients, typically involving the large joints of the extremities.  
  - These patients are usually **over 20 years of age**, with **two-thirds being female**.  
  - **20%** of these arthritic patients also have erythema nodosum.  
  - In **80%** of cases, the arthropathy resolves within **6 weeks**; however, **20%** experience a more **chronic course**, averaging **2.5 years** in duration.

---

## Laboratory Tests

Routine laboratory findings in CSD are **nonspecific** and primarily useful for excluding other diagnoses.  
- During the acute phase, patients may exhibit:  
  - Mildly **elevated white blood cell count**  
  - **Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)**  
- **Blood cultures** are rarely positive with current techniques.  
- **PCR testing** of affected lymph nodes is positive in approximately **30%** of cases.  
- **Serology for *Bartonella henselae***:  
  - Positive in **80–90%** of cases at presentation.  
  - Many initially seronegative patients become positive within **2 to 8 weeks**.  
- **Serologic testing** has replaced the CSD skin test as the **preferred confirmatory method**.

---

## Histopathology

Histopathologic examination of lymph nodes in CSD shows nonspecific changes with three overlapping stages of granuloma formation:  
1. **Lymph node enlargement** with germinal center hypertrophy and cortical thickening.  
2. **Granuloma formation** with infiltration by lymphocytes and epithelioid cells.  
3. **Necrosis** accompanied by neutrophil infiltration.  

These stages may coexist within a single lymph node.  
- **Abscess formation** may also occur.  
- *B. henselae* organisms can be identified in lymph nodes and primary skin lesions, often in **clumps or filamentous forms**, typically located **within or near areas of necrosis**.

### Primary Skin and Conjunctival Lesions
- **Skin lesions** show:  
  - Necrosis of the epidermis and upper dermis  
  - Dermal inflammation ranging from neutrophil and macrophage infiltration to granuloma formation  
- **Conjunctival lesions** exhibit similar features.  
  - In some cases, there is vascular proliferation and a **homogeneous eosinophilic to basophilic granular background**, resembling **bacillary angiomatosis (BA)**.

---

## Differential Diagnosis

### Most Likely
- Atypical Mycobacteria (especially *M. marinum*)  
- Sporotrichosis  

### Consider
- Syphilis  
- Tularemia  
- Primary inoculation tuberculosis  

### Rule Out
- Lymphoma  

---

## <mark>Treatment</mark>

- <mark>**Most cases of CSD resolve spontaneously** without treatment.</mark>  
- <mark>A retrospective study of 202 patients showed that commonly used antibiotics (macrolides, tetracyclines, cephalosporins) were **ineffective** in classic CSD.</mark>  
  <mark>- Despite *in vitro* susceptibility of *B. henselae* to macrolides, tetracyclines, and second- and third-generation cephalosporins, clinical benefit in immunocompetent hosts is limited—likely due to low infectious burden and late initiation of therapy, often after spontaneous improvement has begun.</mark>

### <mark>Azithromycin</mark>
- <mark>In a prospective randomized trial, **5-day azithromycin** treatment:</mark>  
  <mark>- Reduced lymph node volume during the first **30 days**</mark>  
  <mark>- **50%** of treated patients reached **20% of baseline volume** by 1 month vs. **7%** in untreated</mark>  
  <mark>- No significant difference in other symptoms or long-term outcomes</mark>  
  <mark>- Some patients experienced **lymph node enlargement after treatment**</mark>

### <mark>Complicated CSD</mark>
<mark>For **ocular** or **central nervous system** involvement:</mark>  
- <mark>Recommended regimen:</mark>  
  <mark>- **Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily**</mark>  
  <mark>- **Rifampin 300 mg twice daily**</mark>

---

## Trench Fever, Urban Trench Fever, and Bartonella quintana Infections

### Epidemiology
- ***Bartonella quintana*** is the causative agent of **trench fever**, which affected over **1 million soldiers** during **World War I**.  
- In recent decades, *B. quintana* has emerged as a cause of **bacteremia** and **endocarditis**, particularly in urban populations—termed **urban trench fever**—reported in the **United States and France**.

# Antibiotic-Associated Complications and Resistance

Gastrointestinal disturbances and oral mucous membrane lesions are the major problems encountered with alteration of the normal microbial flora. There are numerous other potential untoward reactions to antibiotics—such as renal, hematologic, hepatic, and nervous system toxicity—that may represent acceptable risks if the indications for antibiotic use are compelling. It is the physician's responsibility to be aware of both the common and rare manifestations of antibiotic toxicity and to remain alert for novel adverse effects in individual patients.

## Antibiotic Resistance Due to "R" Factors

Transferable resistance to multiple antibiotics has become a widespread clinical challenge. This resistance is largely mediated by extrachromosomal genetic elements known as R plasmids. Prolonged antibiotic therapy can select for R-factor-carrying strains within the indigenous flora, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract. These resistant bacteria may then transfer their resistance genes to potential pathogens during conjugation. For example, an R plasmid in *E. coli* that confers resistance to chloramphenicol, tetracycline, and kanamycin can be transferred to *Klebsiella* or *Salmonella* species during bacterial mating.

## Topical Antibacterial Agents

Topical antibacterial agents are commonly used to prevent or suppress bacterial growth in open lesions and surgical wounds. However, in sutured dermatologic wounds, topical antibiotics have limited efficacy in reducing infection rates. Topical neomycin and bacitracin frequently cause contact dermatitis, particularly when applied to venous insufficiency ulcers of the lower extremities.

Among the most effective topical antibacterial agents are:
- **Acetic acid (1% to 5%)**: Useful for *Pseudomonas* infections involving the nails and toe web spaces.
- **Bacitracin (500 units per milliliter or gram)**: Effective against superficial infections caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* and streptococci.
- **Neomycin (0.5% ointment)** and **gentamicin (0.17% cream)**: May be beneficial in selected cases requiring local suppression of mixed Gram-negative bacteria.
- **Mupirocin (2% ointment)**: Active against various streptococci and *S. aureus*, including some methicillin-resistant strains.

Several broad-spectrum antiseptics are also available for topical use:
- **Povidone-iodine (Betadine)**: Effective against most Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, though it lacks persistent residual activity on the skin.
- **Chlorhexidine gluconate (4% solution)**: Offers broad antibacterial coverage with prolonged action. An alcohol-based formulation is particularly effective, is minimally absorbed systemically, and is generally non-irritating. These antiseptics can be used prophylactically or to treat superficially infected dermatoses and minor wounds.

## Therapy

### <mark>Therapeutic Options Recommended in Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH)</mark>

<mark>**Main option:**</mark>  
- <mark>Lifelong gluten-free diet (GFD) ± dapsone</mark>

<mark>**Additional options (symptomatic):**</mark>  
- <mark>Sulfasalazine</mark>  
- <mark>Potent topical corticosteroids</mark>  
- <mark>Antihistamines</mark>

---

### <mark>Therapeutic Decisions</mark>

<mark>A lifelong gluten-free diet, with or without dapsone, is the cornerstone of treatment for DH.</mark> <mark>The only causative therapy is a strict GFD, which must be implemented in every case.</mark> <mark>However, initiation of the GFD should occur **only after all diagnostic evaluations are complete**, including serologic testing and skin biopsy for direct immunofluorescence (DIF).</mark>

<mark>All other therapeutic options are **symptomatic** and target skin lesions and pruritus.</mark> <mark>They do not affect the underlying disease process or intestinal involvement and therefore **must not replace** the GFD.</mark> <mark>These may be considered under the following circumstances:</mark>  
1. <mark>Symptoms are intolerable</mark>  
2. <mark>Skin involvement is severe</mark>  
3. <mark>Patient refuses or is unable to adhere to a GFD</mark>  
4. <mark>Disease does not respond to a correctly implemented GFD</mark>

<mark>**Dapsone** is the most effective symptomatic treatment.</mark> <mark>Clinical improvement is typically seen within **3–4 days** of initiation, and this rapid response can support the diagnosis of DH.</mark>  

<mark>Alternative symptomatic therapies—such as sulfasalazine, potent topical corticosteroids, and antihistamines—are significantly less effective.</mark> <mark>These should be considered only if dapsone is contraindicated, not tolerated, or refused by the patient.</mark>

<mark>The therapies mentioned above will be discussed in detail in the following sections.</mark>

---

### Gluten-Free Diet (GFD)

The gluten-free diet is the sole causative treatment for DH. It involves the complete exclusion of gluten-containing cereals:  
- Wheat  
- Rye  
- Barley  
- Oats (unless specifically labeled as gluten-free, due to cross-contamination risks)

These can be replaced with naturally gluten-free sources of complex carbohydrates, such as:  
- Rice  
- Corn  
- Pseudo-cereals: quinoa, millet, sorghum  
- Flours derived from almond, chestnut, coconut, poppy seed, pumpkin seed, or sesame

Other safe foods include:  
- Vegetables  
- Fruits  
- Legumes  
- Dairy products (milk, cheese)  
- Eggs  
- Meat and fish (provided there is no gluten contamination during processing or storage)

**Critical Note:** Patients must **not start a gluten-free diet before diagnosis is confirmed**, as dietary withdrawal of gluten can lead to normalization of serologic markers and histologic findings, thereby complicating accurate diagnosis.

Regulatory standards for labeling foods as "gluten-free" were established by **Commission Regulation (EC) No 41/2009**, which defined criteria for gluten content (≤20 ppm). An updated framework for consumer product labeling was implemented by the European Commission starting **20 July 2016**, improving transparency and safety for patients following a GFD.

# Other dietary recommendations

<mark>The gluten-free diet (GFD) is the foundation of therapy for dermatitis herpetiformis (DH).</mark> <mark>However, patients should avoid excessive iodine intake (e.g., seafood, multivitamin-multimicronutrient supplements) as it may trigger disease relapses, particularly in those on an incomplete GFD.</mark>

# Dapsone

<mark>Dapsone is the first-line drug for symptomatic treatment of DH.</mark> <mark>Although no randomized controlled trials have evaluated its efficacy—except for small case series—there is strong consensus that dapsone is highly effective.</mark> <mark>It remains the most effective treatment for cutaneous symptoms and pruritus until the GFD takes full effect, which may take 6–24 months.</mark> <mark>Skin lesions and itching typically resolve within 3–4 days of starting dapsone, and symptoms usually recur within days of discontinuation.</mark>

<mark>Before initiating dapsone, serum glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH) activity should be assessed to rule out deficiency and prevent hemolytic anemia.</mark> <mark>The starting dose depends on symptom severity.</mark> <mark>A low-dose regimen begins at 25 mg once or twice daily to minimize side effects, with weekly increments of 25 mg until an effective dose is reached, up to a maximum of 200 mg/day.</mark> <mark>For maintenance, a dose of 0.5–1 mg/kg/day is generally sufficient to control pruritus and prevent new lesions.</mark>

# Dietary counselling

All DH patients should be referred to a dietitian to ensure proper implementation of a gluten-free diet, especially if additional dietary modifications are required due to comorbidities.

# <mark>Indications of dapsone treatment in DH patients</mark>

<mark>Dapsone therapy is indicated in the following situations:</mark>

- <mark>Intolerable or severe skin involvement</mark>  
- <mark>Skin manifestations persist despite a strict GFD</mark>  
- <mark>Patient is unwilling or unable to adhere to a GFD</mark>  

<mark>In cases of severe disease and intense pruritus, higher starting doses (e.g., 50 mg twice or three times daily) may be used, provided G6PDH deficiency has been excluded.</mark> <mark>Once clinical remission is achieved, the dose should be tapered to the lowest effective maintenance level.</mark> <mark>If no improvement is observed within one week at a dose ≥150 mg/day, the diagnosis should be re-evaluated or alternative therapies considered.</mark> <mark>A strict and sustained GFD allows for rapid reduction of dapsone dosage, and in most patients, dapsone can eventually be discontinued entirely.</mark>

<mark>For pediatric patients, the initial dose is 1–2 mg/kg orally once daily or in two divided doses, with a maximum single dose of 50 mg.</mark> <mark>The maintenance dose is individualized and typically ranges from 10–25% of the initial effective dose.</mark>

<mark>No dose adjustment is necessary in renal impairment.</mark> <mark>In hepatic impairment, caution is advised, and regular laboratory monitoring is recommended.</mark>

<mark>Dapsone therapy should continue until complete remission is achieved.</mark> <mark>In case of relapse, the dose may be temporarily increased by the patient under medical guidance.</mark> <mark>If a severe relapse occurs after discontinuation, dapsone can be safely restarted.</mark>

## Neurologic and Bone Complications

Neurologic disease has been reported in patients with isolated celiac disease, including epilepsy, ataxia, and dementia; however, confirmation of these findings awaits large epidemiologic studies. Some authors have proposed that patients with dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) may be at higher risk for these neurologic complications due to long-standing gluten ingestion; however, Wills and co-workers found no evidence of immune-mediated neurologic disease in their evaluation of patients with DH.

Patients with untreated celiac disease have an increased frequency of bone loss. Patients with DH often continue on gluten-containing diets, leading to chronic, albeit low-grade, malabsorption. Di Stefano demonstrated significantly reduced bone mineral density in patients with DH who consume gluten. These findings suggest that patients with DH should be closely monitored, and those on gluten-containing diets should be screened for decreased bone density. If reduced bone mineral density is detected, patients should be encouraged to adopt a gluten-free diet.

## Differential Diagnosis

DH may be confused with numerous other conditions due to its pleomorphic manifestations and occasional absence of diagnostic lesions.

### Differential Diagnosis of Dermatitis Herpetiformis

#### Consider
- Eczema  
- Atopic dermatitis  
- Papular urticaria  
- Neurotic excoriations  
- Bullous pemphigoid  
- Pemphigoid gestationis  
- Linear immunoglobulin A dermatosis  

#### Rule Out
- Scabies  

Conditions such as eczema, papular urticaria, neurotic excoriations, pemphigoid, pemphigoid gestationis, erythema multiforme, and other bullous or inflammatory dermatoses can typically be differentiated based on histologic and immunologic findings. Linear IgA disease may resemble DH clinically and histologically but is distinct immunologically. A high index of suspicion is essential, as DH can be diagnosed even in the absence of primary skin lesions by identifying characteristic granular IgA deposits in perilesional, normal-appearing skin.

## <mark>Treatment</mark>

### <mark>Sulfones</mark>

<mark>Diaminodiphenyl sulfone (dapsone), sulfoxone (not available in the United States), and sulfapyridine provide rapid improvement in symptoms and signs of DH.</mark> <mark>Symptom relief may occur within 3 hours to a few days after the first dose, and new lesion formation typically ceases within 1–2 days of starting treatment.</mark> <mark>Exacerbations can occur within hours to days of stopping therapy.</mark> <mark>This rapid response was historically a key diagnostic clue.</mark>

<mark>The preferred treatment for adults is dapsone at an initial dose of 100–150 mg/day (usually administered once daily).</mark> <mark>Some patients may require up to 300–400 mg/day for initial control.</mark> <mark>Patients should be instructed to use the lowest effective dose to control symptoms.</mark> <mark>Not all patients require daily dosing; in rare cases, 25 mg weekly may suffice.</mark>

<mark>Sulfapyridine (1.0–1.5 g/day) is an alternative for patients intolerant to dapsone, elderly individuals, or those with cardiopulmonary comorbidities.</mark> <mark>Dapsone pharmacology, mechanisms of action, adverse effects, and monitoring are detailed in Chapter 226.</mark> <mark>It is important to note that nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can exacerbate DH, even in patients taking dapsone.</mark>

### Gluten-Free Diet

**Effect on the Small Intestine**  
The intestinal lesion in DH responds to gluten withdrawal, with a time course of improvement similar to that seen in celiac disease.

**Effect on the Skin Disease**  
Strict adherence to a gluten-free diet leads to a reduction or complete discontinuation of medication in most (but not all) patients, typically after 5 months to 1 year. These findings confirm earlier results from the study by Fry et al. and have been supported by subsequent research.

# <mark>Histology</mark>

<mark>It is recommended to take a lesional skin biopsy for histopathology.</mark>

<mark>A standardized (buffered) $4\%$ formaldehyde ($10\%$ formalin) solution should be used for storage and transport of the biopsy specimen.</mark>

A $4–5\,\mathrm{mm}$ lesional punch biopsy is recommended. An intact vesicle or small erosion on inflamed skin may be completely excised. In the case of larger blisters, which are rare, it is advised to include a small portion of perilesional skin (approximately $\frac{1}{4}$ of the biopsy) to prevent detachment of the blister roof during processing.

<mark>The histopathological hallmarks of dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) include accumulation of neutrophils forming neutrophilic microabscesses in the dermal papillae.</mark> <mark>Dermal papillary oedema is commonly observed, and subepidermal splitting is present in fully developed lesions.</mark> <mark>The blister cavity typically contains fibrin, polymorphonuclear leukocytes (predominantly neutrophils), and nuclear dust.</mark> <mark>Eosinophils may be present in variable numbers.</mark> <mark>A similar inflammatory infiltrate can also be found in the upper dermis.</mark> <mark>In older lesions, nonspecific changes such as lymphocytic infiltration, fibrosis, and ectatic capillaries may be seen.</mark>

<mark>However, histopathological findings alone cannot differentiate DH from other autoimmune bullous diseases such as linear IgA disease, bullous pemphigoid, anti-p200/laminin $\gamma 1$ pemphigoid, or the inflammatory variant of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.</mark>

# Direct Immunofluorescence Microscopy

<mark>Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) microscopy is the gold-standard laboratory procedure for diagnosing DH.</mark>

<mark>The optimal biopsy site for DIF is non-lesional skin, preferably from a perilesional area or a predilection site such as the extensor surfaces of the elbows, knees, or buttocks.</mark>

DIF can be performed using cryosections examined under a short-arc mercury lamp, blue light-emitting diode (LED) microscopy, or laser scanning confocal microscopy. <mark>The characteristic findings in DH are microgranular or microgranular-fibrillar IgA deposits located at the tips of the dermal papillae and along the dermo-epidermal junction (DEJ).</mark> <mark>These papillary IgA deposits often appear as vertical linear structures resembling "falling snow." With serial sectioning, up to seven different patterns may be observed due to combinations of the three primary deposition patterns.</mark>

In approximately $30\%$ of Japanese patients, a fibrillar IgA deposition pattern has been reported. Both $\mathrm{IgA_1}$ and $\mathrm{IgA_2}$ subclasses can form cutaneous deposits in DH, although $\mathrm{IgA_1}$ is the predominant subclass.

## <mark>Clinical Features and Classification of Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH)</mark>

<mark>All patients with Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) fall along a clinical spectrum of disease, ranging from localized, self-limited forms to life-threatening multisystem involvement.</mark>

### <mark>Cutaneous Manifestations</mark>

<mark>Cutaneous lesions vary depending on the clinical subtype:</mark>

- **Hashimoto-Pritzker disease (HPD)**: Traditionally characterized by the eruption of multiple or solitary elevated, firm, red-brown nodules or flesh-red lesions resembling infantile angiomas. Late papulonodular lesions may have elevated borders and are prone to ulceration. Lesions may increase in size and number during the first few weeks of life, sometimes becoming large before spontaneously resolving. They subsequently form brown crusts, which shed and may leave whitish atrophic scars.  
  <mark>Notably, small reddish-brown crusted papules—resembling chickenpox—are a common presentation of **self-healing LCH**, with spontaneous clearance typically occurring by 2 to 3 months of age.</mark>

- <mark>**Letterer-Siwe disease (LSD) and Hand-Schüller-Christian disease (HSC)**: Cutaneous lesions appear in successive crops, more rapidly in LSD and less so in HSC. On the scalp, lesions may coalesce and mimic **seborrheic dermatitis** or **folliculitis**, often leading to alopecia. In skin folds (retroauricular, axillary, genital), they resemble **intertrigo**.</mark>  
  <mark>Lesions may merge into plaques on the medial chest, mid-back, and temporoparietal areas, occasionally becoming **xanthomatous**.</mark>

### Mucous Membrane Involvement

Mucosal lesions are typically **noduloulcerative** and commonly affect:
- Perioral region
- Gingiva  
  In **eosinophilic granuloma (EG)**, perigenital and perianal regions are frequently involved.

Although mucous membrane lesions are absent in HPD, **oral manifestations** may be the initial sign of LCH and include:
- Non-specific pain
- Aphthous-like ulcers
- Gingival bleeding
- Candidiasis
- Ulceration with tooth loosening
- Premature tooth eruption

### Nail Changes

<mark>Nail abnormalities are associated with a poorer prognosis and include:</mark>
- <mark>Fragile nail plate</mark>
- <mark>Paronychia</mark>
- <mark>Subungual pustules</mark>
- <mark>Nail fold destruction</mark>
- <mark>Onycholysis</mark>
- Subungual hyperkeratosis
- Longitudinal grooving
- Pigmented or purpuric striae of the nail bed

These changes can occur in both children and adults.

### Cutaneous Findings in Elderly Patients

<mark>Skin lesions in older individuals resemble those seen in pediatric cases, supporting the diagnosis of LCH even in adulthood.</mark>

---

## Diagnostic Markers for LCH

Immunohistochemical staining of lesional cells typically shows positivity for:

- **S100 protein**
- **CD1a**
- **CD207 (langerin)**

These markers help confirm the presence of Langerhans cells.

---

## Classification of LCH by Extent of Disease

### Single-System LCH (Restricted Disease)
- **Skin-limited disease** without involvement of other organs  
- **Monostotic bone lesion**, with or without:
  - Diabetes insipidus
  - Adjacent lymph node involvement
  - Rash  
- **Polyostotic bone involvement** (multiple bones or >2 lesions in one bone), with or without:
  - Diabetes insipidus
  - Adjacent lymph node involvement
  - Rash

### Multisystem LCH (Extensive Disease)
- **Visceral organ involvement** (e.g., liver, spleen, lungs, bone marrow), with or without:
  - Bone lesions
  - Diabetes insipidus
  - Lymph node involvement
  - Rash  
  Subdivided based on presence of **organ dysfunction**:
  - Without dysfunction of lungs, liver, or hematopoietic system
  - With dysfunction of lungs, liver, or hematopoietic system (high-risk disease)

---

## Related Physical Findings

Systemic symptoms are common in aggressive forms of LCH and include:
- Malaise
- Weight loss
- Failure to thrive
- Nausea
- Myalgia
- Arthralgia
- Fever

---

## Bone Involvement

Bone lesions are the **most frequent manifestation**, occurring in **80% of LCH cases**.  
Bone involvement as the sole site of disease is observed in **50–60% of patients**, highlighting the skeletal system as a primary target.

# <mark>CUTANEOUS MANIFESTATIONS OF DRUG ABUSE AT A GLANCE</mark>

<mark>Parenteral administration of drugs can lead to skin lesions and eruptions through local or systemic effects, including toxic or hypersensitivity reactions caused by the drug, adulterants, or infectious agents.</mark> <mark>Intravenous drug use often produces characteristic skin findings that may indicate illicit drug use to those familiar with such signs.</mark>

## <mark>DEFINITIONS</mark>

- <mark>**Parenteral drug use**: Administration of drugs via routes other than the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly intravenous, intramuscular, or subcutaneous injection.</mark>
- <mark>**Cutaneous manifestations**: Skin changes including tracks, scars, ulcers, infections, and inflammatory reactions associated with drug injection or systemic effects of abused substances.</mark>

## <mark>COMMONLY ABUSED DRUGS</mark>

- **Cannabis** (marijuana, pot, weed, ganja): Derived from *Cannabis sativa*, it contains delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive compound.
- **Diacetylmorphine** (heroin): A potent opioid that accounts for 90% of opiate abuse in the United States. When injected intravenously, it produces a "rush" within 7–8 seconds; when snorted or smoked, the effect occurs in 10–15 minutes.
- **Cocaine** (coke, blow, snow): A stimulant and topical anesthetic derived from the coca plant. It is commonly used nasally, intravenously, or smoked.
- **Crack cocaine**: The freebase form of cocaine, smoked for rapid and intense euphoria. It is highly addictive.
- **Methamphetamine** (meth, crystal meth, ice): A powerful central nervous system stimulant. When crystallized ("ice"), it is typically inhaled or injected to produce a strong rush.

## <mark>CUTANEOUS SIGNS OF INJECTABLE DRUG ABUSE</mark>

<mark>The pattern and appearance of skin lesions can help identify current or past drug dependency.</mark> <mark>The most specific cutaneous indicators include:</mark>

- <mark>**Track marks**: Linear hyperpigmented scars or indurations along veins, especially in the antecubital fossa, forearm, or dorsum of the hand.</mark>
- <mark>**Puncture wounds**: Small scabs or crusted papules at injection sites.</mark>
- <mark>**Ecchymoses**: Bruising around injection areas.</mark>
- <mark>**Phlebitis**: Inflammation of veins, presenting as tender, erythematous cords.</mark>
- <mark>**Woody dermal induration**: Firm, fibrotic skin changes due to repeated injections and sclerosing phlebitis.</mark>
- <mark>**Cutaneous ulcers**: Often located in atypical or hidden areas (e.g., groin, feet, neck), resulting from poor injection technique, contaminated substances, or vasculitic effects.</mark>
- <mark>**Scars of unknown origin**: Multiple, irregular scars suggestive of self-injection practices.</mark>

## <mark>INFECTIOUS COMPLICATIONS</mark>

<mark>Drug addicts are at increased risk for:</mark>

- <mark>**Blood-borne infections**:</mark>
  <mark>- Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV): Approximately 40% of AIDS-related deaths are linked to drug abuse.</mark>
  <mark>- Hepatitis B and C: About 60% of new hepatitis C cases in the U.S. result from needle sharing.</mark>
    <mark>- One-third of injection drug users become infected with hepatitis C within 6 months of starting injection.</mark>
    <mark>- By 2 years, up to 90% may be infected.</mark>
  <mark>- Hepatitis D (requires HBV co-infection)</mark>
  <mark>- Human T-lymphotropic virus types 1 and 2 (HTLV-1/2)</mark>

- <mark>**Bacterial infections**:</mark>
  <mark>- Predominantly affect skin and soft tissue (e.g., abscesses, cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis).</mark>
  <mark>- Often polymicrobial or caused by antibiotic-resistant organisms (e.g., MRSA).</mark>
  <mark>- Culture-guided antibiotic therapy is essential due to high rates of unusual pathogens and resistance.</mark>

## <mark>ASSOCIATED HEALTH AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS</mark>

- Increased prevalence of sexually transmitted infections (e.g., syphilis, gonorrhea).
- High rates of depression, anxiety, and other psychiatric disorders.
- Accidental injuries, trauma, and overdose.
- Exposure to criminal violence and domestic abuse.
- Societal burdens including:
  - Loss of work productivity
  - Increased crime and incarceration
  - Property damage
  - Economic cost: $143.4 billion in 1998, projected to rise to $204 billion by 2007 (9% attributed to health care costs).

## <mark>CLINICAL RECOGNITION</mark>

The typical appearance of chronic stimulant users ("speed freaks") includes:
- Pale, sagging, sweaty complexion
- Poor hygiene and body odor
- Cachexia
- Dental decay ("meth mouth")
- Skin ulcers and scarring from picking or injection

<mark>Recognition of these cutaneous and systemic signs can aid in early intervention, treatment, and prevention of further complications.</mark>

# HEPATITIS AND THE SKIN

<mark>There may be no visible skin changes in patients with severe liver disease, and conversely, dramatic cutaneous manifestations may develop in those with minimal hepatic dysfunction.</mark>

<mark>Cutaneous striae may appear in patients with chronic hepatitis, regardless of the underlying cause and even before glucocorticoid therapy (see Fig.</mark> 151-1). <mark>Pyoderma gangrenosum, urticaria, vasculitis, acne, scleroderma, and splinter nail hemorrhages can occur, depending on the specific etiology of the hepatitis.</mark>

## Clinical Features of Acute Viral Hepatitis

<mark>The clinical features of infection with the different hepatotropic viruses that cause acute viral hepatitis are similar.</mark> <mark>In the pre-icteric phase, patients typically experience malaise, lethargy, nausea, and abdominal pain.</mark> <mark>A discrete, transient, maculopapular, urticarial, or petechial rash may develop, often accompanied by arthritis or arthralgia.</mark> <mark>These symptoms may worsen with the onset of jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools.</mark> <mark>Malaise and fatigue can persist for weeks or months after resolution of the acute illness.</mark>

### Hepatitis A

Hepatitis A virus is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. Although relapses can occur, hepatitis A does not progress to chronic hepatitis.

### <mark>Hepatitis B</mark>

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is transmitted through percutaneous and permucosal routes. It is endemic in many regions, and healthcare professionals are at increased risk. A recombinant DNA vaccine is available, though it has been associated with cutaneous side effects.

Approximately 5% of HBV-infected individuals become chronic carriers, and up to 90% of infants born to infected mothers develop chronic infection.

There are four main cutaneous associations of hepatitis B:

1. <mark>**Serum sickness-like syndrome** – Occurs in about 10% of patients during the pre-icteric phase of acute HBV infection. Urticaria may be the dominant or only feature, but it is often accompanied by low-grade fever, arthralgia (especially in peripheral joints), proteinuria, and hematuria. Vasculitis may also be present.</mark>

2. <mark>**Cryoglobulinemia** – Both HBV and HCV are associated with cryoglobulinemia, though HCV is more commonly implicated. In HCV infection, mixed cryoglobulinemia is typically type III, and its presence may indicate active viral replication. Clinical features include recurrent purpura, acrocyanosis, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy, peripheral neuropathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Renal involvement is common. Histopathology shows necrotizing vasculitis.</mark>

3. <mark>**Polyarteritis nodosa** – Can occur during acute HBV infection or develop years later. It is associated with circulating immune complexes containing hepatitis B surface antigen and immunoglobulin. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis may be present.</mark>

4. **Papular acrodermatitis of childhood (Gianotti-Crosti syndrome)** – Typically affects children and presents with monomorphic, flat-topped, erythematous papules on the face and limbs. The eruption is usually self-limiting and asymptomatic but may be associated with lymphadenopathy. Other infectious agents and vaccinations have also been linked to this condition.

Sweet syndrome has recently been reported in association with both acute and chronic HBV infection.

### Hepatitis C

Hepatitis C virus (HCV) was historically the leading cause of posttransfusion hepatitis, though screening has significantly reduced new cases.

<mark>Cutaneous manifestations of acute and chronic HCV infection include:</mark>

- <mark>Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (often due to cryoglobulinemia)</mark>
- <mark>Cutaneous necrosis</mark>
- <mark>Pruritus</mark>
- <mark>Acquired angioedema</mark>
- <mark>Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT)</mark>
- <mark>Erythema nodosum</mark>
- <mark>Urticaria</mark>
- <mark>Erythema multiforme</mark>
- <mark>Polyarteritis nodosa</mark>

<mark>**Lichen planus** is more commonly observed in HCV-infected patients, although study results vary regarding the exact incidence.</mark> <mark>An increased frequency of the HLA-DR6 allele has been noted in Italian patients with HCV-associated oral lichen planus, suggesting a role for host genetic factors in this association.</mark>

# <mark>Diagnosis</mark>

## <mark>Clinical diagnosis: The importance of the neonatal period</mark>

<mark>The cutaneous lesions are major criteria for the diagnosis of incontinentia pigmenti (IP).</mark> Four stages are well characterized and summarized in Table 2, along with their main differential diagnoses.

- <mark>**Stage 1 (vesiculopustular stage):** This initial inflammatory stage is characterized by vesicles and pustules, typically appearing in the neonatal period. The lesions are often acral and follow Blaschko’s lines. They may be profuse or limited in number. This stage is highly suggestive of IP when occurring in a female neonate with a linear, acral distribution and spontaneous resolution in early childhood. Eosinophilia is commonly observed during this stage; however, since eosinophilia can be physiological in early infancy, it is considered a minor criterion when associated with Stage 1 lesions.</mark>

- <mark>**Stage 2 (papular-verrucous stage):** This stage usually follows Stage 1 and presents as warty, hyperkeratotic papules or plaques, also distributed along Blaschko’s lines. Histologically, it shows papillomatosis, acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and numerous apoptotic keratinocytes in the epidermis, with dermal infiltration of eosinophils and lymphocytes.</mark>

- <mark>**Stage 3 (hyperpigmented stage):** Characterized by swirling, hyperpigmented macules that follow Blaschko’s lines. These lesions typically appear after the resolution of earlier stages and may persist for years, gradually fading during adolescence.</mark>

- **Stage 4 (hypopigmented stage):** This late stage consists of linear, hypopigmented, and often hairless streaks or patches, predominantly on the limbs. These lesions are permanent and may be subtle, sometimes requiring skin biopsy for confirmation.

Although IP predominantly affects females, it can rarely occur in males. The diagnostic criteria remain valid in male neonates, though the presentation may be more severe.

Spontaneous regression of Stages 1 and 2 is typical within the first months of life. However, late-onset outbreaks—linear and following Blaschko’s lines—have been reported years after the neonatal period, sometimes triggered by viral infections. Therefore, IP should be considered in the differential diagnosis even in older children or adults with clinically suggestive skin lesions.

Histopathological examination is crucial, especially in atypical or late presentations. It is particularly important in cases of subungual verrucous lesions that are painful, to exclude benign or malignant nail tumors.

Cutaneous and scalp manifestations:
- Alopecia may result from scarring due to inflammatory (Stage 1) or verrucous (Stage 2) lesions, typically on the vertex. These areas may be small and inconspicuous.
- Hair, eyelashes, and eyebrows are often thin and sparse. Scalp hair may have a "woolly" texture, though without specific hair shaft abnormalities.
- Nail abnormalities, such as striations or thickening, can occur but are non-specific and not pathognomonic.

## Skin histology

Histological findings support the clinical diagnosis and vary by stage:

- **Stage 1:** Eosinophilic spongiosis, intraepidermal vesicles containing eosinophils, dyskeratotic (apoptotic) keratinocytes, and a dermal infiltrate rich in eosinophils and lymphocytes.
- **Stage 2:** Papillomatosis, acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and persistent apoptotic cells in the epidermis, with dermal eosinophilic infiltration.

The complete absence of minor criteria should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis, as it may suggest an alternative condition.

# Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of dermatitis herpetiformis

## Abstract

<mark>Dermatitis herpetiformis is a rare disease that should be considered the cutaneous expression of a gluten-sensitive enteropathy indistinguishable from celiac disease.</mark> <mark>Dermatitis herpetiformis is often misdiagnosed, and to date, no guidelines for its management have been published in the literature.</mark> These guidelines have been developed for dermatologists by the Group for Cutaneous Immunopathology of the Italian Society of Dermatology and Venereology. They reflect the best available evidence at the time of preparation, along with the clinical experience of the authors and members of the Italian Group for Cutaneous Immunopathology.

<mark>The diagnosis of dermatitis herpetiformis is established through clinical, histological, immunopathological, and serological evaluation.</mark> <mark>A gluten-free diet (GFD) is the treatment of choice.</mark> <mark>Dapsone and/or other medications may be used during the initial phase until the GFD becomes effective.</mark> These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis and management of dermatitis herpetiformis.

## Keywords

celiac disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, diagnosis, guidelines, management, therapy

## Introduction

<mark>Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease characterized by pruritic, polymorphic skin lesions and distinct histopathological and immunopathological features.</mark> <mark>Increasing evidence supports that dermatitis herpetiformis represents the cutaneous manifestation of a gluten-sensitive enteropathy identical to celiac disease.</mark> <mark>Both conditions are multifactorial, involving genetic predisposition and environmental triggers, resulting in specific pathology in the small intestine and skin, respectively.</mark>

<mark>There is a strong association with HLA-DQ2 (present in 80–90% of patients) and HLA-DQ8 (in 10–20% of patients), which is shared by both dermatitis herpetiformis and celiac disease.</mark>

<mark>The disease typically manifests in the third decade of life, although it can occur at any age.</mark> <mark>It predominantly affects Caucasians.</mark> <mark>The reported incidence is 11.5 per 100,000 in Scotland and ranges from 19.6 to 39.2 per 100,000 in Sweden.</mark>

<mark>Patients with dermatitis herpetiformis have an increased risk of immunomediated diseases and associated conditions, including lymphoma.</mark>

## Diagnostic Protocol

Clear and concise diagnostic criteria are essential for accurate identification of dermatitis herpetiformis, ensuring appropriate treatment and long-term monitoring.

<mark>Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation, histology, immunopathology—specifically direct immunofluorescence (DIF)—and serology, including IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) and IgA endomysial antibodies (EMA).</mark>

<mark>While a suggestive clinical picture and positive serologic tests support the diagnosis—and some authors consider anti-tTG testing sufficient—DIF of perilesional (uninvolved) skin remains the gold standard for confirming dermatitis herpetiformis.</mark>

<mark>In cases of negative DIF results, serial sectioning of the biopsy specimen should be performed.</mark> <mark>If results remain negative, a second biopsy should be obtained from clearly uninvolved skin, ensuring the patient is not following a gluten-free diet, which may affect test outcomes.</mark> <mark>Given that false-negative IgA detection is often due to technical issues, DIF should be performed in experienced laboratories to reduce the risk of both false-positive and false-negative results.</mark>

# GUIDELINES

## S2k Guidelines (Consensus Statement) for Diagnosis and Therapy of Dermatitis Herpetiformis  
Initiated by the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV)

## Abstract

**Introduction**  
Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is a chronic, pruritic, gluten-induced skin disorder characterized by subepidermal granular IgA deposition and a variable degree of enteropathy identical to that seen in coeliac disease. To date, there has been no European consensus on the management of DH.

**Methods**  
These guidelines were developed by small subgroups of a guideline committee comprising 26 specialists from various medical disciplines and one patient representative. The committee discussed and voted on the final recommendations during two consensus meetings. The process was supported by the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) in collaboration with the European Dermatology Forum (EDF).

**Results**  
The guidelines provide evidence-based and expert-based recommendations (S2 level) for the diagnosis and management of DH (see Appendix).

**Conclusion**  
These guidelines aim to improve the quality of care for patients with DH and support dermatologists in making informed diagnostic and therapeutic decisions.

## Introduction

### Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH)

#### Definition  
<mark>Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is a chronic, polymorphic, pruritic, gluten-induced skin disorder characterized by subepidermal granular IgA deposition and a variable degree of enteropathy identical to that observed in coeliac disease (CD).</mark> <mark>DH can therefore be considered a distinct cutaneous manifestation of CD, with combined intestinal and skin involvement.</mark>

#### History  
The term *dermatitis herpetiformis* was first introduced in 1884 by Louis Adolphus Duhring, a dermatologist from Philadelphia, who described a chronic skin condition marked by severe pruritus and polymorphic lesions. <mark>The association between DH and systemic involvement, particularly coeliac disease, was first reported by Marks et al.</mark> in 1966, when they identified small intestinal mucosal abnormalities in DH patients. In 1967, Cormane detected immunoglobulins at the dermal-epidermal junction in DH, and two years later, van der Meer identified these as IgA. In 1979, Chorzelski and colleagues distinguished linear IgA disease from DH based on differences in direct immunofluorescence patterns. In 1983, they demonstrated that sera from patients with DH and CD contain IgA autoantibodies against endomysium. In 1990, Karpati et al. analyzed cutaneous immunoglobulins at the ultrastructural level. The key breakthrough came in 1997, when Dieterich et al. identified tissue transglutaminase (TG2) as the autoantigen targeted by anti-endomysial antibodies. Six years later, Sardy et al. identified epidermal transglutaminase (TG3) as the primary autoantigen in DH.

#### Genetic Background  
DH is strongly associated with HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 haplotypes. Approximately 85% of Caucasian DH patients carry HLA-DQ2, with most of the remaining 15% carrying HLA-DQ8. In Japan, a variant of DH with similar skin manifestations but without association to coeliac disease has been described. This variant is characterized by absence of gluten-sensitive enteropathy, lack of HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8, frequent fibrillar IgA deposits in the papillary dermis, and no strong link to autoimmune diseases or lymphomas. Beyond genetic predisposition, environmental factors—particularly high dietary gluten intake—play a crucial role in disease development.

#### Epidemiology  
DH is a rare condition, with a reported prevalence of 10 to 75 per 100,000 individuals and an annual incidence of 1 to 3.5 per 100,000. It is exceptionally rare in Asian populations and less common among African-Americans. Most epidemiological data derive from populations of Northern European descent, both in Europe and North America, where the disease is most prevalent. While adult onset is typical in Northern Europe, childhood onset appears more frequent in Mediterranean countries.

# Small bowel biopsy

<mark>Since dermatitis herpetiformis can be considered the cutaneous counterpart of celiac disease, a proven diagnosis of dermatitis herpetiformis in a patient should serve as a diagnostic indicator for associated small bowel damage.</mark> <mark>Therefore, small bowel biopsy is generally unnecessary in patients with confirmed dermatitis herpetiformis.</mark> <mark>Monitoring diet adherence can be achieved through serological testing and clinical observation of skin lesions, as dermatitis herpetiformis lesions typically recur within a few days of gluten ingestion.</mark>

Indeed, recent evidence suggests that small bowel biopsy is no longer mandatory for diagnosing celiac disease in certain patient subgroups.

# HLA haplotypes testing

<mark>Virtually all patients with dermatitis herpetiformis, like those with celiac disease, carry either HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 haplotypes.</mark> <mark>The presence of these alleles has nearly 100% sensitivity for dermatitis herpetiformis and a very high negative predictive value—meaning that the absence of these alleles effectively rules out celiac disease.</mark>

<mark>HLA testing for DQ2 and DQ8 can therefore be a valuable tool in excluding the diagnosis when clinical, serological, or histological findings are inconclusive.</mark> <mark>However, due to the high prevalence of these alleles in the general population, their specificity for celiac disease or dermatitis herpetiformis is low, limiting their use as a standalone diagnostic test.</mark>

# Screening for autoimmune diseases and associated conditions

Patients with dermatitis herpetiformis have an increased risk of other immune-mediated disorders, warranting routine screening. Recommended tests include:

- Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies (positive in up to 20% of patients)
- Antigastric parietal cell antibodies (positive in 10–25%)
- Antinuclear antibodies
- Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies

These autoantibodies reflect the underlying autoimmune predisposition associated with celiac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis.

Additionally, screening for:
- Thyroid dysfunction (TSH, T3, T4)
- Type 1 diabetes (fasting glucose or HbA1c)

is recommended.

Although earlier studies suggested an increased risk of lymphoma, recent data show no significant increase in lymphoma risk in dermatitis herpetiformis patients compared to the general population. Nonetheless, clinicians should remain vigilant for signs of intestinal or extraintestinal lymphoma.

# Screening first-degree relatives for celiac disease

First-degree relatives of patients with dermatitis herpetiformis or celiac disease have a higher risk of developing celiac disease. While screening symptomatic relatives is clearly beneficial, there is limited evidence supporting routine screening of asymptomatic first-degree relatives.

# Therapy

## <mark>Gluten-free diet (GFD)</mark>

<mark>A gluten-free diet (GFD) is the cornerstone of treatment for both celiac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis, as both the intestinal and cutaneous manifestations are gluten-dependent.</mark>

- <mark>Gastrointestinal symptoms typically improve rapidly on a GFD.</mark>
- <mark>Skin lesions resolve more slowly, with an average of 2 years required for complete clearance.</mark>
- <mark>Skin rash invariably recurs within 12 weeks of gluten reintroduction.</mark>
- <mark>IgA deposits at the dermal-epidermal junction may take several years to disappear with strict dietary adherence and reappear upon gluten exposure, often preceding or accompanying rash recurrence.</mark>

<mark>The toxic cereals belong to the tribe *Triticaceae* and include:</mark>
- Wheat
- Rye
- Barley

<mark>Historically, the gluten-free diet excluded wheat, barley, rye, and oats (mnemonic: BROW).</mark> <mark>However, recent studies indicate that pure, uncontaminated oats (from the *Avena* genus) are safe for most patients with celiac disease or dermatitis herpetiformis.</mark>

<mark>**Important**: Only oats that are certified free from contamination with wheat, barley, or rye should be consumed, as most commercial oats are cross-contaminated.</mark>

# <mark>Mucosal and Cutaneous Lesions</mark>

<mark>The mouth is the most frequent site of involvement in patients with cicatricial pemphigoid and is often the first—and sometimes the only—site affected.</mark> <mark>Lesions commonly involve the gingiva, buccal mucosa, and palate; other sites such as the alveolar ridge, tongue, and lips are also susceptible.</mark> A frequent oral manifestation is **desquamative gingivitis**. <mark>Other lesions may present as tense blisters that rupture easily or as mucosal erosions resulting from epithelial fragility.</mark> <mark>Oral lesions can lead to a delicate white pattern of reticulated scarring.</mark> In severe cases, adhesions may form between the buccal mucosa and alveolar process, around the uvula and tonsillar fossae, and between the tongue and floor of the mouth. <mark>Gingival involvement can result in tissue loss and dental complications, including caries, periodontal ligament damage, and loss of bone mass and teeth.</mark>

Ocular involvement is common in cicatricial pemphigoid and may become sight-threatening. Ocular lesions typically begin as conjunctivitis that progresses insidiously to scarring. Early disease is often subtle and nonspecific, usually starting unilaterally before becoming bilateral over several years. Patients may report burning, dryness, or a foreign-body sensation in one or both eyes; frank blisters on conjunctival surfaces are rarely observed. Early ocular changes are best detected by slit-lamp examination. Because lesions may be localized to the upper tarsal conjunctiva, they can be missed without eyelid eversion. Chronic ocular disease leads to scarring characterized by shortened fornices, **symblepharons** (fibrous adhesions between bulbar and palpebral conjunctival surfaces), and, in severe cases, **ankyloblepharon** (fibrous fusion of the upper and lower eyelids).

A few skin lesions on the upper body are also sometimes noted. Associated symptoms are site-specific, as detailed later.

## Topical and Systemic Treatment Approaches

Topical measures are aimed at supportive care and minimizing exacerbating factors. Systemic treatment includes prednisone, colchicine, and thalidomide.

## Behçet Disease

Behçet disease (see Chap. 167), a rare multisystem disorder most prevalent in Japan, Turkey, and the Middle East, is characterized by oral and genital ulcers, iridocyclitis, and variable presence of synovitis, meningoencephalitis, and cutaneous pustular vasculitis with aphthae. At least two of the other findings are required for diagnosis. The oral ulcerations of Behçet disease are an almost universal finding and often herald the onset of this syndrome. The lesions present as multiple aphthous-like ulcers that heal within a few weeks and recur at least three times per year (Fig. 74-9).

## Cyclic Neutropenia

Cyclic neutropenia, an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by cyclic decreases in the number of circulating neutrophils, presents with ulcerative gingivostomatitis that lasts a few days and recurs at intervals of 21 to 27 days. Progression to periodontal disease with subsequent alveolar bone loss is seen over time. Spontaneous improvement is seen as the neutrophil count recovers, but systemic antibiotic therapy may be required to prevent bone loss.

## <mark>Non-Aphthous Erosions and Ulcers</mark>

<mark>Shallow, painful erosions on the gingiva and buccal mucosa, which at times may be extensive and may lead to ulcerations, occur in pemphigus vulgaris (see Chap.</mark> 52; Fig. <mark>74-10), paraneoplastic pemphigus (see Chap.</mark> <mark>53), and, less frequently, in bullous pemphigoid (see Chap.</mark> 54).

<mark>Virtually all patients with cicatricial pemphigoid (see Chap.</mark> <mark>55) develop mucosal lesions that consist of a desquamative gingivitis with painful erosions on the tongue, buccal and palatal mucosa, and ocular symblepharon.</mark>

<mark>Oral erosions that heal without scarring are commonly seen in both epidermolysis bullosa (EB) simplex and junctional EB (see Chap.</mark> 60). <mark>Patients with dystrophic EB demonstrate the most severe oral involvement.</mark> <mark>In the recessive form, caries, diffuse oral ulceration, scarring, microstomia, vestibular obliteration, and ankyloglossia are frequent findings.</mark> <mark>The dominant form has similar features but demonstrates less severity (see Chap.</mark> 60). Minimizing trauma and optimizing nutrition are paramount, and early referral to dentistry is key in maintaining oral function.

## <mark>EROSIVE GINGIVOSTOMATITIS (DESQUAMATIVE GINGIVITIS)</mark>

<mark>Erosive gingivostomatitis is characterized by inflammation and erythema of the gingiva and represents a nonspecific reaction pattern.</mark> <mark>It may be associated with viral infections or autoimmune, inflammatory, and blistering disorders such as lichen planus (LP), erythema multiforme, pemphigus, and cicatricial pemphigoid.</mark> Gingivitis and periodontitis are specifically excluded from this diagnosis. <mark>Other mucocutaneous sites may also be involved.</mark>

## LICHENOID MUCOSITIS

Lichenoid mucositis presents with reticulated white plaques and painful erythematous erosions on mucosal surfaces. It can result from lichen planus, medications (e.g., nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antihypertensives), contact allergy, or graft-versus-host disease. Identification and management of underlying causes or triggers are essential. If symptoms persist after removing the etiology, treatment may progress from topical steroids to systemic corticosteroids.

## LICHEN PLANUS

Lichen planus (LP) is a common, chronic, inflammatory condition affecting the skin and mucosa, predominantly in adult women. It is characterized by lacy, white patches, plaques, or papules, which may be asymptomatic or painful, and often accompanied by erosions and ulcerations.

## ACUTE NECROTIZING ULCERATIVE GINGIVITIS (TRENCH MOUTH, VINCENT DISEASE)

Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivostomatitis is marked by punched-out ulcers of the interdental papillae. Precipitating factors include stress, poor oral hygiene, nutritional deficiencies, and alcohol or tobacco use. Immunosuppressed individuals, especially those with HIV, are at higher risk. Common features include gingival hemorrhage, severe pain, foul odor, fever, and lymphadenopathy. In advanced cases, it may lead to alveolar bone destruction. Associated microorganisms include *Treponema*, *Selenomonas*, *Bacteroides fusiformis*, *Prevotella intermedia*, and *Borrelia vincentii*. Treatment involves improved oral hygiene, antiseptic rinses, systemic antibiotics, and, in severe cases, surgical debridement.

## GINGIVAL HYPERPLASIA

Gingival hyperplasia refers to enlargement of the free and attached gingiva, particularly the interdental papillae. It may result from infiltration by malignant lymphocytes (e.g., in leukemia), glycogen storage disease type Ib, or medications such as phenytoin, calcium channel blockers, and cyclosporine. Management includes discontinuation of the causative agent if possible, improved oral hygiene, antibiotics, and gingivectomy in moderate to severe cases.

## APHTHOUS ULCERATION (APTHAE, CANKER SORE, RECURRENT APHTHOUS ULCERATION)

Aphthous ulceration is characterized by acute, recurrent, painful ulcers occurring on nonkeratinized oral mucosa. It is the most common cause of oral ulcers, affecting up to 30% of the population. Most individuals experience episodic ulcer development.

## <mark>Erythema Nodosum</mark>

<mark>Erythema nodosum is characterized by a sudden onset of symmetric, tender, erythematous, warm nodules and raised plaques with bilateral distribution, typically located on the anterior aspect of the lower extremities (Figs.</mark> <mark>68-4 and 68-5).</mark> The lesions are most commonly found on the shins. Initially, the nodules appear vivid red or purplish, evolving over several days to a yellow or greenish hue, resembling a deep bruise—a feature known as *erythema contusiforme*. Ulceration does not occur, and healing takes place without atrophy or scarring.

Acute episodes of erythema nodosum are often accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever, fatigue, malaise, arthralgia, headache, abdominal pain, vomiting, cough, or diarrhea. The eruption typically lasts 3 to 6 weeks, and recurrences are common.

Clinical variants such as erythema nodosum migrans, subacute nodular migratory panniculitis of Vilanova and Pinol, and chronic erythema nodosum are now considered part of the spectrum of erythema nodosum rather than distinct entities.

### <mark>Etiology</mark>

<mark>Erythema nodosum is associated with a wide range of underlying conditions, including:</mark>

- <mark>**Infections** (e.g., streptococcal infections—most common in children; also tuberculosis, Yersinia, Mycoplasma, fungal infections)</mark>
- <mark>**Medications** (e.g., sulfonamides, oral contraceptives, penicillins)</mark>
- <mark>**Malignancies** (e.g., lymphoma, leukemia)</mark>
- <mark>**Autoimmune and inflammatory diseases** (e.g., sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease—most common in adults)</mark>
- <mark>**Pregnancy**</mark>
- <mark>**Idiopathic** (a significant number of cases have no identifiable cause)</mark>

<mark>It is regarded as a hypersensitivity reaction to various inciting agents.</mark>

### Histopathology

Erythema nodosum is the classic example of **mostly septal panniculitis without vasculitis**. Key histologic features include:

- Thickened connective tissue septa of the subcutis infiltrated with inflammatory cells extending into periseptal fat.
- Inflammatory infiltrate composition varies with lesion age:
  - **Early lesions**: Predominance of neutrophils.
  - **Late lesions**: Histiocytes, small granulomas, and multinucleated giant cells.
- **Miescher radial granuloma**: A characteristic finding consisting of small, round aggregates of histiocytes arranged radially around a central slit-like cleft. The nature of this cleft remains unknown, with no evidence of endothelial lining on ultrastructural or immunohistochemical studies.
- In older lesions, histiocytes may coalesce into multinucleated giant cells that retain a stellate cleft reminiscent of the Miescher granuloma.
- **Absence of vasculitis** is a critical diagnostic feature.
- Late-stage changes include granulation tissue at the septal-fat interface and fibrosis, but resolution occurs without scarring or atrophy.

### Treatment

Management focuses on identifying and treating the underlying condition.

- Most cases resolve spontaneously within a few weeks.
- Supportive measures such as bed rest may be sufficient.
- Symptomatic relief can be achieved with:
  - **Aspirin**
  - **Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)**
  - **Saturated solution of potassium iodide** (2–10 drops daily), which may accelerate resolution
- **Systemic corticosteroids** are rarely necessary and should be avoided unless absolutely indicated, particularly if an underlying infection has not been ruled out.

# TABLE 153-2 Major Pathologic Differential Diagnosis of Sarcoidosis on Skin Biopsy

- <mark>Tuberculosis</mark>
